soil-bio-091.title: What humus is made of, and why it is hard to say
soil-bio-091.text: Chemists in the 1940s and 1960s tried to take humus apart, and they failed. Their extractants reacted with the organic matter and created artifacts. Humus remains a very complex substance that is still not fully understood. Its core is very large molecules, built partly from lignin and other plant polyphenols and partly from similar molecules made by microbes. Proteins, amino acids and amino sugars attach to this base, giving humus a moderate nitrogen and sulfur content. Radiocarbon dating shows the base, mostly lignin and black carbon, can be very old, while the attachments are much younger. Microbes strip the protein more readily than they break the base, and younger protein may take its place. In the classical view of {{ref:soil-hist-018}}, fully humified humus is amorphous, uniformly dark, spongy and jelly-like. Yet under a light microscope it may still show tiny plant, animal and microbial remains, broken up mechanically but not chemically.

soil-bio-113.title: The detritus food chain, eaten again and again
soil-bio-113.text: Detritivores eat dead matter, but they mostly digest the microbes living on it. In the detritus food chain, or detritus cycle, microbes multiply on detritus and detritivores feed on both. The microbes quickly take up small proteins, lipids and sugars and slowly decompose complex carbohydrates. They take carbon from the detritus but nitrogen and phosphorus from their surroundings. Detritivores digest mainly these protein-rich microbes and excrete the detritus barely changed. Microbes regrow on that dung over several days, and it is eaten again. Each passage thins and fragments it until its complex carbohydrates disappear. Bacteria and fungi recycle the rest.

soil-bio-117.title: The priming effect: feeding soil can speed its decay
soil-bio-117.text: Add fresh organic matter to soil, and the old organic matter may start to disappear faster. This is the priming effect: a change, positive or negative, in how fast soil organic matter decomposes after something is added to soil or {{ref:soil-fert-028}}. Löhnis discovered it in 1926 while studying how {{ref:soil-fert-026}} decomposed. Bingeman named it in 1953, but it was widely disregarded until the 1980s–1990s. Pulsed or continuous inputs of fresh organic matter usually trigger it, and usually it accelerates mineralization. The common explanation is that microbes, fueled by energy and nutrients from the fresh material, become more active. Positive priming speeds mineralization. Negative priming causes the opposite, leaving nitrogen locked up and unavailable. Many things can prime decomposition: fertilizers, plant litter, detritus, root exudates, plowing, and drying and rewetting. Where priming occurs, soil organic matter turns over at least one order of magnitude faster than in the bulk soil. It appears within days or weeks. It is larger in carbon- and nitrogen-rich soils and with larger additions, and it has not been seen in sterile environments. Its mechanisms are more complex than first thought and remain poorly understood. Similar mechanisms may operate in water.

soil-bio-105.title: Humin, the most stubborn part of soil organic matter
soil-bio-105.text: About half of soil organic matter will not dissolve in anything. Soil organic components split into a soluble fraction, largely humic acids, and an insoluble fraction, the humins, which make up about 50%. Humin is that insoluble, carbon-based fraction of giant molecules, the most resistant of the humic substances. It has the greatest molecular weight and darkest color of them. It is insoluble in acids, alkalis and water at any pH, and it resists microbes most. As the most stable form of humus, it may persist for centuries if not millennia. Biorefineries also make humins as by-products of sugar dehydration.

soil-bio-130.title: The hydrogen cycle and the soil that soaks it up
soil-bio-130.text: Soil is where most hydrogen gas leaves the air: biological uptake by soil is the dominant sink of atmospheric H2. The hydrogen cycle is the exchange of hydrogen compounds between living and non-living sources and sinks, centered on molecular hydrogen. Microbes make H2 with hydrogenase and {{ref:soil-fert-101}} enzymes and by fermenting organic matter without oxygen. Over 30% of microbial taxa carry hydrogenase genes. Other organisms use that H2 to reduce CO2 to methane or acetate, sulfate to hydrogen sulfide, or Fe3+ to Fe2+. H2 is an indirect greenhouse gas, because it can hinder the removal of methane from the air.

soil-bio-096.title: Mull, where animals mix the litter into the soil
soil-bio-096.text: Under mull, fallen leaves disappear fast. Mull is a humus form in which burrowing animals mix organic matter thoroughly into the mineral soil. The result is a well-developed, granular A horizon of humus bound to mineral particles, with no thick organic layers and no OH horizon. Earthworms are its most widespread makers. Polydesmida millipedes in Appalachian old-growth forests, darkling beetles in dry regions and burrowing mammals also form mull. It occurs in deciduous forests and grasslands under mild climates with moderate rainfall, on parent materials rich in weatherable minerals. Its plants drop easily decomposed litter with a low ratio of carbon to nitrogen, which releases nutrients instead of locking them up. Fuller decomposition oxidizes organic acids, raising soil pH and base saturation. A positive feedback follows: better litter speeds decomposition and nutrient cycling, which speeds plant growth. Because its litter is quickly buried and bound to minerals, mull ultimately stores more carbon than {{ref:soil-bio-103}} or {{ref:soil-bio-104}}.

soil-bio-104.title: Mor, where litter piles up and fungi rule
soil-bio-104.text: Mor and thick moder were long confused under one name, raw humus. Mor is the humus form of coniferous forests and heaths in which litter decomposes very slowly and piles up on the soil, barely mixing into the mineral soil. Evergreen needles, heath twigs and woody debris rot slowly because of low pH, few nutrients, much lignin, tannin or terpenes, and cool, wet conditions. Bacteria are inactive at low pH and earthworms are absent, so fungi do most of the work. A thick OL horizon lies on an OF horizon matted with roots and fungal hyphae, then a variable OH horizon. The change to mineral soil is sharp, with no A horizon. Organic matter instead leaches in solution through the E horizon to the B horizon, as in podzolization. High C:N and C:P ratios lock up nitrogen and starve plants, which then drop nutrient-poor litter, closing a loop. Ectomycorrhizal and ericoid fungi pass nitrogen straight from the slowly rotting remains to plants. Mor goes with very cold climates, high altitude or latitude, pines and heath, or heavy pollution.

soil-bio-121.title: Glomalin, a soil glue no one has isolated
soil-bio-121.text: In 1996 USDA scientist Sara F. Wright proposed glomalin, a sugar-bearing protein said to coat arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi. The name comes from Glomerales, an order of fungi. It is usually assumed to glue soil into stable aggregates and reduce erosion. A related measure, glomalin-related soil protein (GRSP), correlates strongly with aggregate water stability. GRSP declines when the fungi are removed, hinting at a fungal origin. It takes 7–42 years to biodegrade and is thought to supply up to 30 percent of the carbon in soils where the fungi live. Yet the protein has never been isolated, and its origin and role in storing carbon are disputed.

soil-bio-103.title: Moder, the busy middle ground between mull and mor
soil-bio-103.text: Franz Hartmann placed moder midway between mull and mor. Like mor, it piles partly to fully humified material on top of the mineral soil. Unlike mor, it teems with animal life. Moder is the humus form in which litter decomposes slowly and builds up mainly as the fecal pellets of litter-dwelling invertebrates. Its makers do not burrow: springtails, oribatid mites, millipedes, woodlice, insect larvae, snails, slugs, surface-dwelling earthworms and enchytraeid worms. It forms under conifers, and in deciduous forests where acidity and poor litter keep earthworms and bacteria scarce. Moder is highly acidic and rich in carbon, with a high C:N ratio and low cation exchange capacity, nitrogen and base saturation. Still, more nutrients are available than in mor. Its hallmark is a loose OF horizon full of droppings and animal activity. Its thin A horizon is built of sub-millimeter feces, mostly from enchytraeids. Fine tree roots and their ectomycorrhizal hyphae penetrate these feces to capture nutrients.

soil-bio-131.title: Kerogen, organic matter locked in rock
soil-bio-131.text: Most of Earth's organic compounds are not in living things but in rock. Kerogen, the solid, insoluble organic matter of sedimentary rocks, exceeds the organic content of living matter 10,000-fold. It forms from dead plants, algae and microorganisms compressed and heated over geological time. Labile kerogen yields mainly oil, refractory kerogen mainly gas, and inert kerogen no hydrocarbons, only graphite. Humic kerogen comes from land plants, from precursors such as cellulose, lignin, terpenes and phenols. With coal, kerogen is one source of natural organic matter in groundwater.

soil-bio-119.title: Four fractions of soil organic matter
soil-bio-119.text: About 15% of soil organic matter is alive, including roots. The other 85% falls into four groups, in order of decreasing ease of decomposition. First come simple compounds dissolved in soil water, such as organic acids, sugars, amino acids and root mucilages; they turn over in less than 12 months. Particulate organic matter comes next. Humus, amorphous colloidal particles under 53 microns, is usually the largest share, 45 to 75%, and persists for decades. Resistant organic matter, such as charcoal, graphite and coal, lasts hundreds of years and improves structure, water holding and cation exchange.

soil-bio-128.title: Dissolved organic matter, soil's most mobile carbon
soil-bio-128.text: Some of the carbon in soil travels with the water. Dissolved organic matter (DOM) is the fraction that passes a filter with pores of about 0.22 to 0.7 micrometers; its carbon is dissolved organic carbon (DOC). In soil it comes from rain, litter, crop residues, manure, root exudates and decaying organic matter. It is one of the most active and mobile carbon pools, affecting soil charge, acid-base reactions, nutrient retention and the trapping of heavy metals. Clays and iron and aluminum oxides hold it. Leached DOC can reach the water table in well-drained soils, and under mor it moves from the E to the B horizon.

soil-bio-102.title: How humus forms shift with forests, farms and climate
soil-bio-102.text: A site's humus form is not fixed. It shifts with vegetation, land use, pollution and climate. During forest succession organic horizons thicken, from mull in early stages towards moder under mature stands; in old natural forests the two alternate. Converting conifer forest to broadleaf turns moder into mull, and conifer plantations on deciduous land do the reverse. Farming that encourages earthworms can create a mull-like form called agri-mull. Pollution that harms earthworms slows decomposition and pushes the form towards mor, so humus forms offer a cheap early warning of contamination. Warmth favors mull, yet it also speeds microbial decomposition, depleting humus and leaving many soils with a negative carbon balance. A 3 °C rise in alpine grasslands reduced soil humus content. Earthworms disperse slowly, so change can lag, and adding them to turn moder into mull has given mixed results.

soil-bio-100.title: Reading the layers of a humus form
soil-bio-100.text: A hand lens and a knife are enough to read a humus form. Along a knife-cut profile, or by hand from a small block of soil, its horizons follow the stages of litter decay and its mixing into mineral matter. On top is the OL horizon, called Oi in the American system: recognizable leaves or needles that animals have not yet fragmented. Only in the most active mull does it vanish for part of the year. Below lies the OF horizon (Oe), litter chewed by feeding animals and mixed with their fecal pellets. Those pellets range from 30-50 micrometers, from enchytraeids, mites and springtails, to 1-2 millimeters, from earthworms and millipedes. Next is the OH horizon (Oa). It is humus formed once plant remains are no longer visible but not yet mixed with mineral matter, often piled-up fecal pellets. Fine roots and ericoid mycorrhizal fungi there can decompose resistant organic matter and pass its nitrogen to the host plant. In the A horizon, burrowing animals mix organic and mineral matter. Larger animals build aggregates over 250 μm, smaller ones aggregates under 250 μm. The E horizon is a white or ashy, carbon-poor layer through which water, solutes, clay and humus are leached.

soil-bio-097.title: Amphi humus, mull and moder stacked together
soil-bio-097.text: Amphi humus, also called twin mull or amphimull, combines moder-like OF and OH horizons with a mull-like granular A horizon. It occurs where seasons contrast sharply. Summer drought in Mediterranean areas and winter frost in mountains drive earthworms deeper, so activity at different depths peaks at different times of year. Amphi shows that litter thickness alone cannot identify a humus form: the mineral horizon below must be examined too. With two carbon sinks side by side, it may store carbon better than any other humus form.

soil-bio-099.title: HUMUSICA, a worldwide key to humus forms
soil-bio-099.text: National humus classifications mostly describe temperate forests. HUMUSICA, created in the 2010s, covers terrestrial, semi-aquatic, cultivated and man-made environments worldwide. It sorts humus forms by both their structure and their function. Mull, moder and mor become humus systems, or humus interaction systems. Each holds several humus forms that differ in the thickness of their organic and mineral-organic horizons. Mull splits into Eumull, Mesomull, Oligomull and Dysmull, while Amphimull is a system of its own. It has also been suggested that the pedon be split into humipedon, copedon and lithopedon, in decreasing order of biological influence and speed of change.

soil-bio-098.title: Tangel, the deep organic mat on mountain limestone
soil-bio-098.text: On hard limestone and dolomite in cold, humid mountains, organic matter can pile up as a layer up to 1 m thick. Kubiëna named it the tangel layer. Tangel humus rests this mat on rock, with little or no A horizon. Tangel and mor are two pathways of organic matter in such mountains: tangel on alkaline substrates, mor on acidic ones. Its biology is little studied. One northern Alps study found microbial activity, fungi and bacteria falling with depth while archaea increased.

soil-bio-122.title: Is glomalin real? The extraction behind the debate
soil-bio-122.text: No one has ever isolated glomalin itself. What exists is a heat-and-citrate extraction yielding material reactive to the antibody Mab32B11, first detected by ELISA in 1987. Labs without ELISA measure a crude extract with the Bradford assay, so three different things share one name. The extraction heats citrate to 121 °C for at least an hour. Analysis in 2010 showed it also pulls out humic substances, so the glue effect may not be glomalin. Proteomics finds most extracted proteins are not of mycorrhizal origin. The fungi can even cause net losses of carbon from soil. Sources still disagree on whether glomalin exists and how much carbon it holds.

soil-bio-123.title: Canopy soils, gardens in the treetops
soil-bio-123.text: Soil can form high above the ground. Where branches and crevices in a forest canopy trap leaves and fine branches, the matter weathers into canopy, or arboreal, soil. In some temperate rainforests it reaches 30 cm deep. Epiphytes, plants rooted on trees, grow in it, add organic material and speed its development. Older canopies and lower positions gather more. Soils high up face extreme swings of sun, wind and moisture. They abound in southern-hemisphere temperate rainforests that stayed largely ice-free during the Last Glacial Maximum. Logging and climate change destroy them faster than they can be studied.

soil-bio-101.title: The Humus Index, a number for humus forms
soil-bio-101.text: The Humus Index turns humus forms into a ranked number. It covers all lowland terrestrial humus forms, ordered by the growing share of organic layers in the profile. It runs along gradients such as Eumull to Dysmull and Hemimoder to Dysmoder. Because it can be rank-correlated with soil or vegetation measurements, it serves as an indicator of soil condition or forest stand development. It covaries with fertility, forest management, tree age, pollution level and plant species richness.

soil-bio-127.title: Litter quality: why some leaves rot faster
soil-bio-127.text: Not all leaves rot at the same pace. Litter quality is the chemical make-up of fallen plant material, such as its nutrient, lignin and tannin content. It governs how fast litter decomposes and which humus form develops. Nutrient-rich litter decomposes faster, slowing as those nutrients fall. Deciduous 'improving' litter goes with mull. It decomposes easily, has a low C:N ratio, releases nutrients and encourages bioturbation. Coniferous 'acidifying' or 'recalcitrant' litter goes with moder or even mor. Its low pH, low nutrients and high lignin, tannin or terpene contents slow decay. Tannins protect plants from insects and infection, but they also lower soil pH and can lock nitrogen into resistant tannin-protein complexes. A positive feedback ties it together: better litter speeds decomposition, nutrient cycling and plant growth.

soil-bio-092.title: The soil continuum model and the case against humus
soil-bio-092.text: Some soil scientists doubt that humus, as textbooks describe it, exists at all. The soil continuum model holds that soil organic matter is a continuum of progressively decomposing compounds, not a set of distinct, persistent humic substances. Its starting point is a blurry line. The boundary between humus and other soil organic matter is ambiguous, so some authors contest the terms humus, humic substances and humification. Supporters say the evidence does not show large, persistent humic molecules forming in soils. Critics of the humic-substance concept add that the alkali extracts used to isolate it misrepresent soil organic matter. Others push back. They hold that humus has distinct properties, mostly from its richness in functional groups, the reactive clusters of atoms on its molecules. Those properties, they argue, justify keeping the term. The humification theory persists in the field and in textbooks. Attempts to redefine humic substances have produced many conflicting definitions. The question stays open: soil scientists still disagree on whether humus and humic substances are distinct materials or artifacts of extraction.

soil-bio-124.title: Nitrogen cycling high in the canopy
soil-bio-124.text: Canopy soils release nitrogen faster than the forest floor does. That makes them a main nitrogen source for epiphytes at different heights. Their gross production of nitrate is about the same as or lower than on the forest floor, possibly because canopy soils are more acidic. Nitrogen capture there depends on environmental variation, especially seasonal changes in tropical rainforests. Storing nutrients in the canopy cycles them tightly and keeps them from washing out of the ecosystem. That cycling also affects the fertility of the forest floor below.

soil-bio-129.title: White-rot fungi, the lignin breakers
soil-bio-129.text: Leaves or needles bleached pale in the litter layer may be the work of white-rot fungi. These wood- and litter-decaying fungi break down lignin, one of the main precursors of humus. Lignin decays very slowly, mainly through white-rot fungi and actinomycetes. Brown-rot fungi, by contrast, decompose cellulose and hemicellulose and leave lignin behind. By cutting the lignin and tannin in residues, white-rot fungi and bacteria make them more palatable to earthworms, which helps form mull.

reviews.organic-matter-humus-and-decomposition: This chapter followed fallen litter from the forest floor to the oldest humus. Fungi and bacteria digest it outside their bodies, while earthworms, millipedes and other animals fragment and churn it. Most of it is mineralized into carbon dioxide and nutrients such as ammonium and phosphate that roots take up again. Part is humified instead, into humus that holds water and nutrients and may last for centuries. Litter quality and soil animals decide which humus form a site develops, from earthworm-mixed mull through moder to mor, where fungi slowly work through acid litter that piles up.
